utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. D'Ascoli -- oh, I do beg your pardon. We have Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Dr. Shukri Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a pleasure to see you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Me too, to see Your Honours. [Interpretation] We said that whenever there are some administrative issues to be raised that we would do so before this Trial Chamber. We're dealing with the same old problem. I don't think that it cannot be solved, but as time goes by it seems that it is more and more difficult to solve it. It's a technical issue regarding the use of the computer by the accused, using an external hard disk in the UN Detention Unit. We first received assurances that this would be resolved, but it has not yet been solved. That is why my colleague, Mr. Djurdjic, and myself have problems preparing for our defence because of the huge amount of documents that we have to supply to our client on DVDs and CDs, and he cannot -- he cannot find his way around this mass of material using various search engines. He has asked for a number of facilities, but the only way to solve it is for him to be allowed to use an external hard drive, and several accused in the Detention Unit have been using it for a long time, and I can't see why his case is different. I beg you, Your Honours, to give this problem due attention and to take it seriously because we don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the accused who are using an external hard drive?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can recall, the first external hard drive - and this is to the knowledge of my client - was received by General Perisic, but you have to take that with a pinch of salt. This is what I heard from the client. And several other people have also been using external hard drives. I don't know what the problem is. I've talked to experts in the field and they told me it's a very easy thing to solve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would be surprised to learn that external hard drives are available in the Detention Unit because of major security problems in the past from that use, and I think that is the fundamental problem that is in the way of your client's issues. So I have - when this was raised many weeks ago - received a detailed report about the matter and changes were then made to help your client, but they did not go as far as an external hard drive. And the problem there is security. The matter will be raised again, and I will learn whether there is a difference, and I will also inquire whether other accused are having this facility. But if they are, that doesn't automatically mean that your client will because it may be that there are continuing difficulties. The matter will be looked at. We will do our best to ensure that, consistent with security, every facility is available to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, since we're on administrative matters, may I just mention quickly in court that a witness scheduled for next week, K89, has reported to us through the Victims and Witnesses Unit that he has -- without going into his personal details, he has had issues with a member of his family and can't come as scheduled. So he will have to be pulled out of the list for next week. I will, of course, send a written notification to the Chamber and the parties, but I thought I should announce it at the very earliest opportunity. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Stamp. We would assume then that a later witness will be brought forward if there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll make efforts to do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Djordjevic is kindly asked to switch off his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Djordjevic, it's been noted that your microphone is still switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Gerxhaliu. Could you please state your full name --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: My name is Shukri Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What is your age, Dr. Gerxhaliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: 55, about to be 56. I was born in 1953.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were you born, Dr. Gerxhaliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I was born in Studime e Poshteme, in the vicinity of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And where do you live now, Dr. Gerxhaliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I still live in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, in February 2000 did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you had the chance to review the statement recently?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe you made a number of corrections to this statement when this was reviewed recently. I will read out to you a number of corrections, and if you could please confirm that they are indeed correct. For your assistance, I will hand you out a copy of your statement that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: May I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number for the statement is 2275, but I proceed to -- I intend to proceed through the statement fairly quickly, to just read out the corrections and obtain the witness's confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 24 of your statement you said: "From where we were hiding, I saw about ten vehicles coming up the road from Studime e Poshteme ..." Your correction read, that this sentence should read: "From where we were hiding, I saw about ten vehicles coming up from the road from Studime e Poshteme towards Studime e Eperme." The seventh sentence of paragraph 24 reads: "We have no fuel and it is clear up here." This sentence should read: "We have no fuel and it is clear up here. We have mopped up the terrain ..." Is this correction correct, Mr. Gerxhaliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, these corrections are correct. This is how it was, because the convoy came from the direction --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gerxhaliu, I will just stop you there. We will go into your evidence in a moment. I would like to now move on to the next paragraph, where you made another correction. This is paragraph 25. And the first sentence reads: "When the Serb soldiers had gone, Halil and I walked up towards Studime e Eperme." This sentence should read: "When the Serb policemen and soldiers had gone, Halil and I walked up towards Studime e Eperme." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct, because once they left we saw that there was nobody near so we went into hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. Having made these changes to your statement, are you satisfied that your statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the statement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, did you testify in the case of Milutinovic et al. in August 2006?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gerxhaliu, you made some changes to your testimony. I will read them out for you. At page 2507, line 14, of your testimony in Milutinovic, you said that the date was incorrectly noted, that the correct date should be the 2nd of May instead of the 2nd of April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And at page 2520, line 3 of the Milutinovic testimony that you gave, you said that the number of Albanian girls killed was incorrectly noted and that the number should be eight Albanian girls. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, not nine but eight. That was the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And at page 2521, line 9, of the transcript in Milutinovic, you said that the three persons mentioned as my uncle and his sons was incorrectly noted, and that this should be my uncle Xhemajl; his cousin Selatin; and his son Shaban. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My uncle was called Xhemajl, and his son Selatin, and his son Shaban.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gerxhaliu, having made these corrections to your testimony, if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the witness's transcript in the Milutinovic case, which is 65 ter 5130, into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to read out the witness's in-court summary. The witness is a Kosovo Albanian doctor. He describes events leading up to the convoy killings on the Studime Gorge road on 2 May 1999. On 28 or 29 May 1999, Serb forces launched an offensive from the Rashice area outside the village of Studime e Eperme in Vucitrn municipality. Villagers fled to the hills to escape. Serb forces burned houses in Studime e Poshteme to prevent villagers from returning. On or about 2 May 1999, Serb forces broke through the KLA lines in the northern areas of Meljenica and Llap and advanced south in the direction of the village of Studime e Eperme. The witness estimates that approximately 40.000 refugees formed a convoy and headed down the Studime Gorge road in the direction of Vucitrn town. Serb forces advanced from the north and shelled the convoy. Serb forces also fired from positions in Rashice and Saracak south of the convoy. Some of these refugees in the convoy were killed by the forces, others beaten, and valuables extorted from them. The witness hid and survived the massacre and states that the police units were involved in this operation. That's the end of the in-court summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, I'd now like to ask you some questions about your statement. In paragraph 5 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm going to have to stop for a moment. I don't seem to be receiving translation in -- my B/C/S translation does not seem to be coming through. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you speak about the patients whom you treated. Could you tell us, please, who your patients were around about October 1998.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: During October 1998 in the health clinic of Vushtrri, I used to treat all the patients that came there. When I returned in the evening or whenever I had time after work, I used to go to the area controlled under the KLA and treated all the patients irrespective of whether they were KLA members or civilians. I administered help to everyone who needed it --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. Now, in paragraph 6 of your statement you say that approximately 80 per cent of the Vucitrn municipality was under KLA control.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance I would like to place 0038 on the ELMO. I think it may be easier for the witness to mark the map if it were placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You also say in your statement at paragraph 6 that the Serbs were stationed at a strategic position in the area of Rashice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just a moment, Dr. Gerxhaliu. I'm sorry that there's a slight delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the area of Vucitrn, and I believe the map needs to be turned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, I have a few questions to ask you about the map. Could you please mark for us the areas that were under KLA control that you refer to in your statement. A line would do, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I want to say that Rashice is a neighbourhood in Studime e Poshteme. It's situated on a rather higher terrain compared to the others. This is Studime e Poshteme, this is Rashice neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if you could draw for us the line that shows the area of KLA control in that area around Rashice.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is Studime e Eperme, this is Studime e Poshteme. It's somewhere here where the division line was. Goes to Saracak e Eperm, then Samadrexhe. The line should be here, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Because Samadrexhe was the check-point of the Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, let me stop you there, please. So just to clarify, the line that you're referring to is the line towards the top of the page. Could you then cancel off the lines that are not correct. Yes, just cancel it off. You can just -- are you able to cancel off the line, please. Thank you. So based on what you have cancelled, we see one long line running across the page going to Samadrexha. If I could stop you from drawing any more, I have a few more questions before we move on, Dr. Gerxhaliu. Now, this line that you have drawn on this page, where was the area of KLA control, was it above the line or below the line?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Above was the area controlled by the KLA, whereas this area under this line was under the control of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please mark that line with an A. If you could just place a letter A above the line you have just drawn.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there an area of KLA control below the railway tracks that you see on this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move the map up just a little bit, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, this is the railway line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is the railway line --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you now draw a line to show the area of KLA control below the railway line, as you say.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is where they were, approximately this must have been the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you place the letter B beside this line.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And to clarify, Dr. Gerxhaliu, was the area of KLA control below this line that you marked B or above this line?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It was here from Cicavica and all these villages were under the control of the KLA. This part, the railway and all these parts were controlled by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify again, Dr. Gerxhaliu, are you saying that the area below the line marked B was controlled by the KLA? And by "below," I mean to the right.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: -- from this line, all this area below was under the control of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what about the area between the two lines that you have marked, so the area between lines A and B, who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This zone was controlled by the Serb forces or the former Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We will move away from the map for a moment. I will leave it on the ELMO because the witness will be marking it further later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, if I could take you back to your statement, please. You say that round about 28th and 29th of March, the Serbs launched an offensive from Rashice, and I believe you have marked Rashice on the map with an R. You say many of the local people left the hills to escape the shooting and shelling and the Serbs then burned the houses in Studime e Poshteme to prevent people from returning. Dr. Gerxhaliu, how do you know that these Serbs burned the houses in Studime e Poshteme?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The day I was still in the town, in the clinic, and we received information that an offensive had been launched. We left work earlier than usual. When I went in the direction of my home, my family members had abandoned the house because villages Begaj and the upper neighbourhood of Rashice were the target of a Serb-launched offensive. The combined Serb forces had entered the place and ordered the villagers to flee, had plundered it of its valuable assets, and had set fire to most of the houses, with the exception of one or two --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: -- and I saw them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- and could I ask you where -- in which village did you live in Vucitrn municipality?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I lived in Studime e Poshteme, where I live today. We called the neighbourhood the Gerxhaliu neighbourhood in Studime e Poshteme where I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to take you to the events on the 2nd of May, 1999, and this is at paragraph 11 of your statement. In this paragraph you say that you were ordered to leave the area because the Serbs had broken the front line in Llap and Meljenica and that you decided to leave Vucitrn. You set out the planned route that your family took. This again is in paragraph 11, and that a convoy was formed. What I would like you to do now, Dr. Gerxhaliu, is turn back to the map you just marked and show us the direction that the convoy took on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, we were at Sllakovc. There was one of KLA's field hospitals here, bigger compared to other field hospitals. In the area of Shala --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, I apologise, but I will have to stop you. If you could just mark for us the direction that the convoy headed in from Sllakovc that you've just circled.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: From Sllakovc, it headed in the direction of Ceceli, here is Ceceli. From Ceceli we went to Studime e Eperme, here is it, and from there we headed towards Studime e Poshteme. Somewhere here the convoy stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could perhaps circle the whole route that you have just drawn for us, if you could circle the whole route and I would like you to place the letter C beside that big circle that you are going to draw around that whole route that you have just drawn for us. Yes, just the route that you have drawn for us now, a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's great. And a C beside it.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in paragraph 12 of your statement, if we could turn back to the statement, you say that you set off around 1.00 p.m. on the 2nd of May and that the Serbs were advancing from the north and were shelling in your direction, which was pushing your group south. Could you tell us, Why is it that you stopped at Studime e Eperme at around 3.00 p.m., as you say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: We stopped there because not only from the back where the Serb forces were, but also the forces positioned at the Rashice hill were shelling in the direction of the convoy. There was shooting, there was shelling, so the convoy could not proceed. There was a hill nearby, and you could see very well the terrain from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, you mentioned that there was shelling from the Rashice hill. Could you place the letter D beside this hill that you referred to, or has that already been marked?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No, just the letter D to show the area that the shelling was heading from.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And where had the convoy stopped?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The convoy stopped here near this hill --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can you place --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: -- and they could not see us behind this hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you place a letter E just by the hill where the convoy stopped.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also mentioned that there was shelling from the north. Are you able to mark the direction from which you heard or saw the shelling from the north? Is that visible on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the map could be moved down a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb forces had taken up positions in Llap, Podujeve municipality, and Meljenica; and they had also set up positions in a location behind us. They were shooting in the direction of Sllakovc. I was amongst the last tractors of the convoy and there were shrapnels flying all around that place above our heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gerxhaliu, you've just drawn an arrow. Does that arrow show --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: They came from this direction. The arrow shows the direction they came from, from Llap, Podujeve municipality, and from this other place. And they were shooting from these two directions in the direction of Sllakovc.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just place the alphabet E beside the arrow that you've just drawn.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I think letter E was placed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Shall I mark this with E as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No, please place an F. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to take you back to your statement, please. You describe, from paragraph 15 onwards, events that you experienced at the convoy. Now you say at paragraph 15 that around 5.00 p.m. a large number of Serb military and paramilitary approached the convoy from the north. Could you tell us what members of these -- of this group did to those in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I was somewhere in the middle of the convoy. They -- I was here at the location marked with E, somewhere in the middle of the convoy. They came from behind. There were combined forces, police, military, paramilitary. They were well coordinated and had all their units there. They approached the tractor three or four times. In the beginning they would ask for Deutschemarks, then when people would run out of money they would start to beat them brutally and ultimately kill them. So group after group they repeated the same pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, what happened to your brother-in-law, Halil Basholli?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Halil Basholli is my wife's brother. He was driving the tractor. They made him get off the tractor, beat him until there was no money left on him. He was brutally beaten. Then when we realised that the other group would come and do the same thing, because the police was a little bit further, the military too, so we decided to get off the tractor and go into hiding. We went to take shelter in the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. By "we," who do you mean? Who did you take shelter with in the stream?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Myself, Halil, and two or three other persons. I don't know who they were; but Halil and myself, we took shelter in the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 21 you speak about leaving the trailer and heading towards the stream and that when you jumped off from the trailer you landed on top of a dead body. You looked down and you saw it was your cousin Haki Gerxhaliu. Dr. Gerxhaliu, could you tell us how Haki Gerxhaliu had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, he was dead. At that time when I jumped off the trailer of the tractor, I jumped on his body because his tractor was behind my tractor. There were other bodies, corpses, there, but I recognised his and then I just continued to the left side in the direction of the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. And before you headed off to the stream, did you see anyone else at the convoy being killed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You could hear shooting on all sides. My tractor was semi-covered and in a way you could see only the part behind the tractor, the northern part. Two or three tractors further, someone approached an elderly couple. The man said to him in Serbo-Croatian, Please don't kill my son. He got married today. And they replied, Then we will celebrate together. And in front of their eyes, they executed him. So I still have in my memory these words in B/C/S, Please don't kill my son. He got married today. And then they told him, We will celebrate now, and they executed him. Nexhip and his son was executed together with two or three other persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. I'd now like to take you to paragraph 24 of your statement which speaks about events later in the day when the survivors of the convoy moved on. You say that you saw a number of vehicles heading up the road from Studime e Poshteme. Could you describe those vehicles for us, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There was a mixture of vehicles. Halil and I, as we were hiding in bushes, trying to hide for them not to see us, we heard them talking between themselves. It was a clear night. I recognised them. First it was a Stojadin make, a police car, whereas the other vehicles were APCs. So they said something to the effect of mopping up the terrain. I heard one of the officers reporting, saying, Army, we did mop up the terrain. We've ran out of fuel and we have to go back, and this is what they did. They turned their vehicles and went towards the direction they initially came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. And after these individuals left, you say at paragraph 25 that you and Halil walked up towards Studime e Eperme. When you arrived there, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Studime e Eperme was burning. Smoke was coming out. We could hardly breathe. The whole village was in flames. One could hear the cry of the cattle that were burning alive, horses and other animals. It was a terrible site, to see the whole village in flames. We went through this smoke in an area further up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And apart from the animals that were being burned -- that were burning and the village being in flames, at paragraph 25 you refer to a number of victims that were mainly men and that there were also five or six women as well. Can you describe the condition these victims were in when you arrived at the village?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This happened after we rested a while because we were worn out from that long night. On the next day, on the 3rd of May, we returned, went back, to see what had happened, whether someone was still alive. When we went there, I saw on the way -- along the way I saw a lot of corpses, men, women, children, and others. The KLA had taken its positions, and in the morning the KLA had come to collect the corpses and was prepared to bury them. When I went near to the burial place, because they needed any help they could get, there was someone from the military police of the KLA, which was a special unit of the KLA, in uniforms and in their duties. This person gave me a list of the victims. It was an approximate list, and he asked me whether I knew the victims. And in the list I saw also my name written. He said that's me -- he said yeah, You are the doctor, and he crossed out my name from the list and he was happy that I was still alive. Then they told me to go back to Sllakovc, to the hospital which was not completely burned, to continue my work and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. I'll now take you to paragraph 35 of your statement where you speak about going to Montenegro in early June. You describe passing through a number of check-points and you refer to the check-point in Zvecane as the most problematic check-points. Can you tell us what happened to the identification cards of those travelling with you at this check-point?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: At that check-point, it was very hard for us to cross through it, even though the bus had Serbian licence plates. They didn't have any doubts about that, but when we went there they came into the bus to check us. They told me, You have to pass the paraffin test to see whether I had been carrying any weapons before --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, if I could just take you back to my question: What was it that happened to the identification cards at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, those documents that were issued in Albanian language by the Ministry of Interior of Kosova then, they tore them up and threw them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gerxhaliu. At this stage, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: But I would like to tender the map that is on the ELMO into evidence, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked version of 65 ter 00038 would be assigned P00514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber has received the statement and the transcript of the earlier evidence of the doctor. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, do you have some cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I, Your Honour, say a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that when I came here to testify in the Milosevic and Milutinovic case, in the context of this statement was the event of 31st of May where the family of my cousin Selatin and my uncle Xhemajl were killed. And I wish that this part of my evidence be incorporated in my statement because now I was not asked about that. So I would kindly ask you to include that part of my evidence into my testimony because it was a very bitter event indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may be a little confused by the procedure we are following, but the whole of your statement and the whole of your evidence in the last trial is now before us. It's been tendered early in your evidence today, and that includes in detail all that you've said about that particular incident, which no doubt is very, very firmly in your mind of the deaths of so many of your family. We have that, we have read it, and we are familiar with it. Because we must hear over 120 witnesses, we are therefore receiving these statements and then just supplementing them with some particular observations. Don't think that we haven't your full story before us; we have. So your request has already been met by what Ms. Gopalan has tendered. Mr. Djordjevic will now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will just need a couple of minutes to get ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you some questions as the Defence counsel of the accused, Djordjevic, in this case in order to get at the truth and to learn everything that you have to tell us. In your statement of the 17th of February, 2000 - and you've told us today that you went through it - at page 2, paragraph 2, you note that on the 26th of March, 1999, an armed Serb paramilitary came to the hospital in Vucitrn where you worked and then the director, also an ethnic Serb, fired you and other Albanian colleagues. Can you tell us, first of all, did you yourself see this Serb paramilitary when he came into the hospital building with your own eyes? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I want to comment on that a little bit. Yes, I saw him with my own eyes, and that in the cellar of the hospital there was -- there were arms, weapons. It was used as a depot. And there -- on top of the building, there was a 24-hour guard to survey the terrain. That particular day, on the 26th of March, he came there armed and was standing in the corridor. The director, Ranko Milenkovic, said to us to go home. I said, Why should I go home or we go home, what have we done? He said there was an order from above, and he used the Serbian word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this oral order from your director, Mr. Milenkovic, were any other explanations given and was there any written document indicating that your employment was terminated? So I'm asking you whether then, or at any point afterwards, you received a decision terminating your employment in that institution?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive any documents, any letters, only that oral order, the explanation that there was an order from above to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At what time of day did this armed paramilitary person come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It was about 10.00 I think. I remember very well that moment. There was an older lady, Serbian lady, waiting at the door for me to visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Doctor, so we'll talk about that later. So at around 10.00. Could you tell me, were you close to him and were you able to see him speak to the director, and did he speak only to the director or perhaps also to you or perhaps some other of your colleagues of Albanian ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That paramilitary stood there in a threatening manner. He didn't utter a word, he simply stood there in the corridor, whoever that paramilitary was. And there were many other paramilitaries, police, army forces from there to the commune. And so there was this guard on top of the building and this depot in the cellar full of weapons. They were brought there earlier. So this person simply stood there on the left side of the corridor leaning against the wall, armed. So when the director said to us, Mr. Milenkovic, that we should leave, of course there was nothing else for us to do. I was the last to leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please explain to me, how did you divine that this order from high up came through this armed person? Could it not have been the case that your director received this order by some other means? That's why I asked you whether he spoke to you or any of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I cannot assume anything. I simply quote what the director said to me, Mr. Milenkovic. He said, You should leave. We have received orders from above, "odozgo" he said. So after I checked this old woman, I took the stethoscope and we left the hospital together with this elderly woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gist of my question is this: Why did you make this conclusion? How did you establish this link between the order from your director, the oral termination of your employment, with the arrival of this person? So can I conclude, then, that you did not see this person speak to your director?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I don't think there is any room for discussion there, whether the paramilitary talked with the director or not; this I don't know. I only know that he was there, and he was armed; and when the director said to me to leave, I had to obey his words even though I didn't know what he knew. I -- if I failed to obey him, I might have suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You say that even before that when this person arrived and while this person was there, the military was present in the hospital, various paramilitaries, the police, it was always as a matter of course. Doctor, how were you able to conclude, then, that this armed person was a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan. Just a moment, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would just like a reference for the Defence counsel's last question where he says: "You say even before when this person arrived and while this person was there the military was present in the hospital, various paramilitaries, the police, it was all as a matter of course." If I could have a reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where are you gathering that from, Mr. Djordjevic, is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a little while before I asked this question the witness said that there were quite a few soldiers there, and my question followed one of the answers. You can see it in the transcript, the LiveNote transcript. He said that there was a guard post in the hospital, that there was an ammunition depot in the basement that was guarded, and that they were soldiers and paramilitaries all around the place. And my question followed after his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of most of that having been said, Mr. Djordjevic. I'm sorry, I may have missed it, but -- certainly there were arms in the basement and a lookout on the roof, but beyond that I don't think the rest of this was said. Perhaps you might -- if you want to clarify with the witness whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, lest we should waste our time let me phrase the question in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any troops, military troops, around the health care centre, and was there an observation post on the roof of the hospital, were there ammunition and weapons depots in the basement guarded by various troops?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the hospital, there was the police academy of the Ministry of Interior of Serbia at that time, and there were always close by such forces. But, as I said earlier, there was a guard on top for a month or so and there were arms in the basement, but we didn't dare go closer to those places. The Serbs told us, Don't you dare go up to the roof and don't you dare go down to the cellar, to the basement. So we knew that, that there was a lookout 24 hours on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see what kind of troops, police, and paramilitaries there were, what exactly did you see, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Where? Do you mean there, in the corridor, where the paramilitary was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Doctor. You were telling us about places that were out of bounds for you, where the Serbs told you not to go, like for instance the basement. So I'm asking you: Who was on the roof? Do you know that? Who stood guard in the basement? Did you see only those people from the police academy or did you also see members of some other units around the hospital, military police, or something else? That's what I want to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry to interrupt again, Your Honours, but there are a number of questions put by the Defence in his last series of questions. I've counted three here at least, and I wonder whether we could clarify for the witness which questions he should be answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we would move more quickly, Mr. Djordjevic, if you asked one question at a time. It would make it easier for the witness then to respond to that one question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, the reason why I asked this question was to expedite matters. Perhaps the Prosecution believes that the best course of action would be for me not to ask any questions, but that's not possible. And that's why I asked the witness whether he saw anybody else apart from the police. That's what I asked. We're now wasting time, and I expect an answer. So were there any members of the military, paramilitaries, or anybody else in and around the hospital apart from the police? I tried to be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your question extended over several subjects. The Chamber is asking you to ask one question at a time so that we can move quickly. If you could deal with your questions that way, the witness will be able to answer more quickly, and we will, I hope, move more speedily. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members -- well, whom did you see around the hospital before this person arrived on that day and after that day, members of what units?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There was movement on a daily basis. As I said, the hospital is situated between the police academy building and the police station. That's where it is to this day. So these were combined units, military, paramilitary. The police was standing guard duty on the roof, whereas downstairs we didn't go. We didn't know who was guarding the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. The question that I asked earlier and that has remained unanswered: What led you to conclude that the person who -- whom you saw in a hospital corridor, that person that was armed, that this was a member of a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: His appearance. His hair was longer than a usual policeman. He was not shaven, so he did resemble a paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Can you tell us if at any point after that you received a written document from your institution, the hospital where you worked, about the termination of your employment. Did you receive any such document, a decision terminating your employment?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: As I said, I was only told orally about the termination of my employment. I never received anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me how many Serb doctors were there in the hospital, apart from you and you were an ethnic Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There were two Serbian dentists, two Serbian doctors, and some nurses -- about five or six I would say in total, less than ten. Now I don't remember the exact number. Ten years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, could you please tell me how many Albanians were there employed in the Vucitrn medical centre apart from you, doctors and nurses and other medical staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I need to elaborate here. In the early 1980s when I got this employment, the structure was the following. 80 per cent of the whole medical staff were Albanians, 20 per cent Serbian. In the 1990s, however, the structure changed 60 to 40, 60 Albanian and 40 per cent Serbian. The Albanians were being removed from their jobs for different reasons. So the structure, the ratio, kept changing. At the time when I was dismissed, it was the -- the ratio was 60 to 40. So there was this constant pressure for this ratio to be changed. The number of Serb employees increased constantly. Serbs were coming as refugees from Bosnia, Croatia, and once they graduated from secondary school, they got employment; Albanians on the other side, their diplomas were not valid, they couldn't get employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now my question is: How many doctors, medical doctors, were there? I'm not asking about staff with only secondary education. How many doctors were there, Albanian doctors?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I would say about 30 in total, doctors and dentists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question, Doctor, is: Did you remain on good terms with some of your Serb colleagues, doctors, who worked in the Vucitrn medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Personally I had good relations and cooperation with all doctors, especially with Natalia Tasi, she was from Croatia. She was a diabetic and she couldn't see well, so I always helped her when she was taking the blood pressure of her patients because she could not read it. So in general, my relations were good with all the doctors and especially with Natalia. As I said, she couldn't see well and I helped her while she was taking the blood pressure of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I ask you this question is because now I want to ask you when was the last time, before you were told not to come back to work, that you received your salary; and do you know what the situation was with the other doctors who were not Albanian and who were not told to leave the Vucitrn medical centre. So when did you receive your last salary and when did they receive their salaries?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The last salary, I don't remember before the war but after the war, once the war was over, someone brought us the salaries in Serbian Dinars. I have not mentioned this in my statement, but it is true that we received the salaries in Dinars after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for your frank answer. My next question is: Did your colleague, the director -- well, were you on good terms with him before he told you that you were fired?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Of course. He was stomatologist. He was appointed by the municipality at that post of director. I was in good relations with him. He minded his own business, I minded mine. He was working as a dentist, as I said, so in general we had good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you this question. So at the time when he told you not to come to work -- or at any point after that, did he tell you the reasons, any reasons, apart from the one that you've shared with us, that he had received the orders to do so from the higher up?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No other reason. This was the last word. I went downstairs, gave the old Serbian lady, who was my patient, a prescription, and left the building together with her; and I didn't see him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is a good time for our technical break, and that is why I would like to make a break in my cross-examination and continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If this is a convenient time, Mr. Djordjevic, we will have the first break now. We must do that for our tapes to be rewound, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, when did you return to Vucitrn from Montenegro, to your home, to the town?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Around 17th, 18th, or 19th, I don't remember the exact date, June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you stayed there ever since, in Vucitrn, in your hometown?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, in Studime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please tell me how many of your colleagues, non-Albanians, remained in the medical centre after June.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: When I returned in June -- are you talking about doctors?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The doctors.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: When I returned after the war, I didn't see any of them there. I heard that they packed their things and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the other medical staff, non-Albanians I mean?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There are Roma and Muslims, but no Serbs -- I mean in the medical centre where I work. There are also Turks there, but no Serbs, and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, let's please determine an important difference in your testimony, in your previous statements, and what you've testified about today; and what you've said today differs slightly from the rest. I would like to highlight for your benefit what it's all about and to hear your comments. You said today that on the 26th of May you received an oral termination of your employment and that you never returned to the medical centre. I think it's on page 22 of today's transcript, lines 14 to 21.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It's not the 26th of May. It's the 26th of March. I don't know if it was your mistake or an interpretation mistake, but it's the 26th of March, two days after the beginning of the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If I said "26th of May," then I made the mistake. Thank you for rectifying that. However, in your examination-in-chief by my learned friend Gopalan, answering one of her questions you responded - and that's on page 12 of today's transcript, lines 19 to 25 - that on the 28th of March you were still in town, that you were at work in your clinic, that you went home and did not find anybody of your family because they had left their home before that, and then you left north. Could you please clarify and specify what is true, that you -- on the 26th of March you were fired and never went back to clinic, or is it true that on the 28th of March you were still in your clinic and then came back, found nobody, and then left town? Which of the two are true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I stated in my statement and in my testimony - I don't know the interpretation you got - but it was impossible for me to go back to the medical centre after the 26th of March because the road was blocked. During these two days, I moved about along the stream, in the mountain, to the KLA hospital in Sllakovc. It was impossible to go back to our house until April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up on the screen, please, today's transcript, page 12, lines 19 to 25; and page 13, lines 1 to 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you read English? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So please take a look at this screen at your response to my learned friend from the Prosecution. Please take a look at the transcript. You said that on the 28th you went home from the clinic and this is why I'm asking you whether you made a mistake, given that you repeated now that on the 26th it was the end of your dealings with the hospital. Let us just clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is a mistake. After the 26th, two days after the NATO bombing started, we left and we didn't go back to the medical centre. I've already said in the past that this was two days after the NATO bombing began. I moved about in the area I described, but it was impossible for me to go back to the medical centre. How can you possibly go back when you -- your life is threatened?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Doctor. My next question is this: We've come to the point where you discussed this elderly woman who was your patient, who you examined, and after which you left the clinic and you said that you never came back. You said that she was your patient. My question is: Had you known that woman from before, the Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: She visited the medical centre very often. She had problems with her kidneys and her heart, so she came frequently for a visit, for opinion. On this day she came for a prescription, for a repeat prescription. She wanted to get a new prescription to get her drugs from the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where she lived, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Somewhere in Vushtrri. She was living nearby. I don't know where exactly, but not far from there. I don't know her address, but I know that she lived in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And she told you, as you recount in your statement, that you were on the list of 7.000 people in Vucitrn that they intended to kill. Is this piece of information about the 7.000 people to be killed in Vucitrn true? Did you interpret this correctly, 7.000 people in Vucitrn, a list of 7.000 people?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I gave her the prescription and she thanked me by asking me, Are you scared? And I said, No, I'm not scared. I only did good deeds for everyone. So I believe there will be someone among Serbs who will defend me, and she replied, she said, This is not correct. Be careful. I heard that the meeting was held and you are amongst those 7.000 people, intellectuals, who will be killed and that the whole area will be mopped up and inhabited by refugees from Bosnia, Croatia, and other places. So I thanked her back and I became more careful, and I consider that in a way she saved my life. I thanked her in my thoughts many times because I had no other opportunity to meet her again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of your statement you said: She said in day-time you treated patients but over-night you would treat KLA. This doesn't sound friendly warning. Could you please explain why she did so, and where did she get this information from?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is what she told me. She heard that in a meeting that was held someone had mentioned my name, Dr. Gerxhaliu during the day is like an angel, whereas in the evening he goes to the terrorists to tend to their wounds, and that's why he will be punished, for his activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph and during your testimony you did say that during night-time you would go to treat KLA wounded and other people in the territory controlled by the KLA. Let me conclude, therefore, then that "they," as you refer to them and she also referred to them as "they," and we believe that these are Serb forces, had information that you were treating KLA soldiers. Am I right in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Of course they did. This is what she confirmed with her words when she warned me, and that's why I became more careful later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And this is why later on you left Vucitrn because you realised that your life was threatened directly by the Serbs, given that they had obtained information that you were treating what they saw as terrorists of the KLA. Is this the reading of the situation after you received this information from that lady?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how it turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My next question is: You said that during the nights you would go to KLA-controlled areas to provide medical assistance to KLA fighters and other people because that population could not come to Vucitrn because they would be killed there. Doctor, please tell us, until the 26th of May, did you have any cases where somebody would come to the medical centre in Vucitrn, coming from KLA-controlled territories, to seek medical assistance and being liquidated or killed before the 26th of May, being killed in the medical centre or around it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you meant to say the 26th of March in that -- you said "May" again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake. [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 26th of March and after that, the Serbian check-points in Dakovce village, which is on the road from Vushtrri to Prishtina, and then in Samadrexha, in the Llazoviq neighbourhood and other check-points, civilians who lived in the area controlled by the KLA and who passed through these check-points were maltreated, some of them might even have been killed. I wasn't able to see everything for myself, but as I stated in my testimony in the Milosevic and Milutinovic trial and today, you will find even nowadays persons who suffered the consequences of the beating and the torture at these check-points. So people were scared to pass through these check-points, and that's why I had to go to them, to treat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, may I conclude after your answer that you do not have direct knowledge that anybody was murdered at the check-point en route to seek medical assistance, those genuinely sick people who needed to see a doctor in Vucitrn? You do not have any immediate knowledge about that; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Personally I don't have such information. People who deal with human rights and freedoms have these records. My main duty and task was to treat those who needed my help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Would you tell me, please, the medical documentation, the so-called medical charts - I don't know what the appropriate English term is to be clear for everybody in the courtroom - was that preserved in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You're referring to the period before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm refer to medical documentation before the 24th of March, 1999. Was that preserved?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: When we returned after the war, we didn't find anything. Everything was thrown away and had disappeared. The medical centre that existed before the war was taken over by the internationals. It was rebuilt and turned into a hospital. So we didn't find anything from these medical charts dating back from the period before the war. We found some personal documentation of Serb colleagues like working permits and stuff like that, and we sent them those documents. However, from medical charts we didn't find anything. As you know, I didn't return immediately after Montenegro to Kosova, but when I did I saw many papers thrown away, torn apart, so nothing from the personal documentation, medical documentation of our patients had remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the identity of this elderly woman that you -- was your patient and visited you frequently?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I don't remember her name, but I know how she looked. She wasn't very tall. She was wearing a scarf on her head. I don't remember her name. I had over 80 patients, but I do remember her face. I do remember her health condition, the therapy she needed, and so forth. I also stated in my statement that it's unfortunate that I don't remember her name. I went to Grablje [phoen] village, which is a Serbian village, to look for her to thank her in person, but I didn't find her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You touched upon something that was about to be my next question. You said that you did not see her after the war. So she was not from Vucitrn, she was rather from the village of Grablje. Thank you for clarifying that --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, no, she was from Vushtrri. She was a woman from town. She had always lived in town. Grablje is a village in Vushtrri municipality nearby, but she was from the town itself. She had an apartment or a house, I don't know exactly. As I said, I didn't know her address. I didn't show interest in finding out the address while she was my patient, but she was from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because you mentioned that you went to Grablje with the intention of going there to thank her, and this is why I asked you about that. So she lived in town. That's what we clarified just now. Thank you. I seek some patience from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please bring up on the screen Exhibit D002-5233. This is the Serbian version or B/C/S version, and could we please -- could we show -- juxtapose 2 -- D002-5235 in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document, Doctor? Please -- do you see the second paragraph which starts with a dash and says: "In the area of responsibility of Kosovska Mitrovica," et cetera, et cetera, can you read the whole paragraph and comment on it, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On which screen is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation. I can see that you're not saying whether you can see it or not. Let me just see what's actually ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the Serbo-Croatian language? 006 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same in the English language. So: "In the area of responsibility of Kosovska Mitrovica on the 24th of September, 1998, in the afternoon hours, a group of three Siptars from the village of Samodreza as representatives of the village went on a tractor to the terrorists in the immediate vicinity of the village of Cecelija in order to convince them to stop with the attacks and to surrender their weapons." Do I have to repeat anything?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: "The terrorists physically abused them, beat them up, destroyed their tractor and made them go back to their village, threatening that they would kill them if they tried the same thing again." Are you familiar with this incident?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, I have no information about such an incident. I already said during the Milutinovic et al. trial and now I'm saying: Give me the names of the persons involved, as you are saying, because this falls outside the scope of my statement. I didn't have any time to deal with everything. You might probably ask the Council for Human Rights, they have been following closely -- more closely everything. I am more involved in professional things. If someone came to me to ask for help, I might have known. So I don't have anything to say about something which I don't know. I haven't heard, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now I ask you for your indulgence as we wait for the exhibit that we're going to need to be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can, perhaps it would be better because I'm not sure I heard from my colleague Mr. Djurdjic that there was a problem with zooming in on this map, it's the document 5244 on the 65 ter list -- in fact, I believe it's Exhibit -- it's 0586767 [as interpreted] in fact, but the 65 ter number is 54 -- is 5244. So if there is a problem with this map, if we can't show on this map what I need, then I will ask questions regarding another map that has already been admitted into evidence. It's a Prosecution document. If we could please have that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the map that the Prosecution showed you, you marked the territory that was under the control of the KLA. This map is now shown to you in its basic format and you can see the railway tracks passing by Vucitrn. My question: You said that 80 per cent of the territory was KLA controlled, so I will conclude that this meant all of the territory apart from major communications or roads that were held by the Serbian forces. And now I'm talking about railway tracks. Was it controlled by the KLA anywhere, either to the north-west or to the south-east of Vucitrn because it runs diagonally as we can see on this map? So was any stretch of that railroad controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I already drew a similar line and explained that the railway line, the city, the highway Prishtina-Mitrovice were always under the control of the Serb forces. I didn't hear that the KLA had it under its control. But below it, all these villages, Cicavica and others, above Studime and others, they were settlements; and I think that this 20 per cent was controlled by the KLA. As I said, the city and its periphery were under the control of the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the Registrar to assist the witness so that he could circle the area controlled by the Serbs with the electronic pen, since apparently it was smaller and it will be easier for the witness to do this on this map.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I already drew a line. This map is very small. I can't see it properly. I can't find the places where the Serb forces were stationed. I can't see Samadrexha or others. It was here, the line, along this territory under the KLA, and here the other line under the control of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask you to zoom in at the area around Vucitrn to the north up to the village of Velika Kicic and Smrekovnica. And to the south we can see them, we can look at the map as it is now. So the lower bottom of the map where Vucitrn is, if we could zoom in on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to see better now?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I can see it better. From Gojbulja, Mirac [phoen], and here between Pasops [phoen] and Konjic [phoen], wait a little bit, please. I can't find Studime e Poshteme. Maybe it's here. I hope I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Donja Sudimlja is to the right of Vucitrn. So could you please circle the area that was controlled by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Here I think. It's Gornja Sudimlja, Donja Sudimlja --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can't zoom in now without losing the markings that have been made. We can zoom in and start the markings all over again if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this is a problem and this is important for the Defence, I would like to ask you to put this map on the ELMO. It's going to be much more accurate than to do it on the screen. The map is now upside down, perhaps if we could put it so that it's ... Now I would like us to put Vucitrn in the middle of what we see here --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, from what I see on the screen, it appears to me that this map has been marked with highlights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There certainly is marking on the map, yes. It's in black what I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: As I recall, the version I saw yesterday did not have any markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor is right. The markings in yellow were done by the Defence in order to be able to locate the places that are mentioned in the witness's statement and nothing else. The black markings, I really don't know what that is. I didn't make the markings, but I myself highlighted the place names that were mentioned by the witness. But if we can't do it on this map, we don't have an unmarked copy of the map. Because I want the witness to circle the areas around Vucitrn that were held by the Serbian forces, if it's possible and if the Prosecution does not object, given that we have this problem, the situation. I don't think that it's crucial in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will take no notice of the present markings which are in black and yellow. The witness I believe will be marking in red and we can follow his markings on the map if that will help you, Mr. Djordjevic, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, because the only question that I have regarding this map is for the witness to circle the areas that were controlled by the Serbian forces, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first map it was even clearer. Here it's not so clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps if the witness can put the map in front of him, circle it, and then put it back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first map it's easier for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we're now going to try and zoom in electronically and get a clearer map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that the map but without the markings that was already marked by the witness be marked now, and then we can admit it into evidence. So if we could look at the previous map, I don't have the number for it, but Ms. O'Leary will help me, it's P514 but without the markings because the marked map has been admitted into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... strain now, Mr. Djordjevic. I think that will be something that the doctor can see more readily and you may want him to mark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that he put markings on this map, that's what I suggested. But if the witness finds it easier to make the markings on a different map, then I agree with that too. But all I want him is to mark the area controlled by the Serbian forces which was 20 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's easier for me to do that on the first map, here. I'm trying to do it now here. I'm a doctor, as you know, and I'm not so good at maps, but I'll try. The Serb forces were in Studime, Lower Studime, Saracak, Samadrexha, in Dumnice, lower Dumnice, they were here at Gojbulja, Smrekonica, and this would be the line. This part below was controlled by the Yugoslav Serbian forces. The remainder up to Llap, up to here, was controlled by KLA forces. Here the railway, as I said, was under Serb forces, Pantine below Delak [phoen], below Sitarice, Nevolane, Preluze, I can't see Preluze, it's somewhere here. That would constitute approximately the line that was under KLA, whereas this part here, between these two red lines, was controlled - at least this is what I thought accounting for some 20 per cent more or less, that's my estimation. You might verify it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing this map anymore, but I would like to have it tendered -- I would like to tender it into evidence with the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The markings made in 65 ter 05244, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing I said to the Prosecutor earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- would be assigned D00069, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is now an exhibit, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Veskovica also controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Veskovice -- Veskovce?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Vesekovc, yes, until the 2nd of May, yes. I'm talking of Vesekovc which is above Sllakovc, Sllakovc, Vesekovc, all that area was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
