utterances.text: In late March and early April was Svracak also controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The two Saracaks were not under the KLA control. There were Serb inhabitants there, and it was under the control of the Serb forces, Saracak e Eperm, Studime, Lower Studime were under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, in late April did Serbs still hold the Svracaks?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, they had under their control Studime and Saracak. There was a Serb check-point that now and again shelled the area along with that Lower Studime. There were always Serb forces in those two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. In paragraph 6, it's the same paragraph, you say that many people had gone into the village -- into the mountains to evade gun-fire and shelling. Can you explain to me why these people did not go to Vucitrn in order to avoid gun-fire and shelling? Because as far as I understand there was no shelling and no shooting there.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The population was driven out of the whole city and gathered in Dardania neighbourhood near the cemetery. There was no room for all of them. Studime Gorge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or stream, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was 2, 3 metres deep and it was a better position for them to go. Whoever wanted to go there wanted -- went there because everybody wanted to save their lives. That's why they went there. Some others were driven out, as I said, of their homes and went to the cemetery; and a massacre occurred there on the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... when I say that you went into the mountains to work in the field hospitals that the KLA had there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I worked in the KLA hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the KLA hospitals at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: When the area was under the KLA control, there was a hospital in Bajgora, Kovacic, but the main one was in Sllakovc, where I spent most of my time. It was a two-storey building. It was -- there was greater space, and we could -- we had the necessary facilities to accommodate the injured, so this is where I worked mostly. It now become a museum hospital even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, tell me, what was your role in setting up the health care system for the KLA members in the field? Was there a hierarchy? Were you the only doctor or were there several?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Sometimes I worked alone. Sometimes colleagues came to help me. From Llap they came to me. Sometimes I went there to help them. There was no hierarchy. We worked on a voluntary basis wanting to provide assistance to whoever needed it. The surgeons came there after the 16th of May, they did their job; but when there was no surgeon around, I had to do the work of a gynaecologist, pediatrician, or surgeon. I simply tried to treat all the patients that came there, trying to do my best, without making any distinction whether -- if I had to deal with injured, infected people, simply sick people, elderly sick, children. I tried to help them, to render my contribution under the Hippocratic oath, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I respect this, but my question has to do with hierarchy and perhaps it wasn't phrased that well. But you will agree with me that providing medical care in wartime, obtaining the resources necessary for the work of you doctors is not so easy. Who was in charge of that? Who decided what would be obtained and where and how this would be organised?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, as I said, it was a voluntary work. Whoever could, brought supplies. Someone who came with the family members brought whatever they had. I gave whatever I had. It was a voluntary work. There was -- nothing was done on an organised way, but people simply tried to help out in providing assistance to the sick people, to the injured. The population brought medical supplies, medicaments. I found a few when I went there, but we used them. From the Llap Operational Zone which was bordering Serbia, sometimes they brought us supplies. They had more supplies than us, and often they -- people from Llap brought us such medical supplies that we needed. I don't know where they found them, they bought them or -- we were lacking them mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You called those hospitals KLA field hospitals. Were you a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, since I worked there I was a KLA member. I already said this, even in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: KLA field hospitals, so does this mean that those hospitals were within the then-KLA system? Were they controlled by the Kosovo Liberation Army in their entirety?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The KLA had one goal: To protect us, to inform us in cases when the front line was broken through. If -- in order for us to get ready and move to some other place, safer place, otherwise we didn't have any other role in our work. As I said, we were doing a voluntary work due to the circumstances that were created by the former regime, everybody tried to do his bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Given evidence from witnesses we had before, more competent, but since you were a member of the KLA, I ask you this: Was the KLA a well-set-up organisation from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Look here, as far as organisation and structuring go, they are not part of my work. As I said, I was involved in the logistical part of it, and I focused only on my work. The KLA had its command. There were these zones, operational zones, in the context of the Shale Operational Zone was the place where I worked, and there was the zone from the north, from Studime, Saracak, and above. But there was another brigade, 142, which operated in the southern part of Vushtrri, Cicavica and around it, but we communicated more with Llap. But between 141 and 142 Brigade there was Vushtrri, where the Serb forces were located, which prevented us from communicating directly -- but here in the hospital we didn't have much time to deal with such things because we wanted to have -- to find supplies, to survive, to provide assistance to the injured, to the sick people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I asked you this, of course being mindful of your location, because of the statement that you provided and still dealing with this in paragraph 11 you said: "On the 2nd of May, 1999, an order came for the KLA to transfer because the Serbs had broken through the front line at Llap and Meljenica." So an order came for the KLA to transfer. Do you know who was the responsible person in the area of responsibility and who could issue such an order from among the KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This was not an order issued by commanders as such. This was more of an information, a message, conveyed to us by the soldiers in the hospital who told us that the combat position in Meljenica, Majdan, in the Llap and Shale Operational Zones, both in the north-western part and south-eastern part have -- are advancing and we need to evacuate. So this was not an order, this was an information, a message conveyed to us, so that we could move before they got there first. So it took time to remove the wounded, to prepare everything. So I was amongst the last to leave, and just before we left, we had a discussion. KLA was a quite democratic organisation. They wouldn't impose anything on you. They -- my family wanted to come with me, to remain with me, so I was free to remain with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood very well what you said and understood that you were not ordered by anybody, that you did so because you had received such information. But you say - and I read it out to you and you can see for yourself - in your statement on the 2nd of May, 1999, the order came for the KLA to move, not the hospital, the KLA because the Serbs had broken through the front line in Llap and Meljenica. This is how the English version reads. The Serbian version reads. This is what you stated in 2000 of course, but now I'm asking you: Do you remember who the order for the KLA to move came from? Do you know who was the responsible person in the zone of responsibility in that area where you worked in the field hospitals, which brigade? Who was the commander? Or was this something coming from the top level again, this order for the KLA to move?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: As for the orders coming from military structures, the military personnel knows that better. We were the logistics part. We worked on a voluntary basis. We just received this message, this news, and we acted appropriately. As for the KLA structure, they have their own orders, I don't know what they were. They left in the direction of Dumnice, whereas the convoy left on the right side towards Ceceli. I know that the KLA took with them the wounded KLA members, whereas the civilians took with them their ill family members. The headquarters where the command, the KLA command was, I never visited it. I didn't have time to visit it. I was all the time in the hospital tending to my patients. So I cannot talk about something that I don't know. I can only tell you that the distance between the field hospital and the KLA command was quite big. They had their own military stuff to do, and I had my own stuff to do to look after the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, am I right if I conclude now that what is stated in paragraph 11 was never uttered by you and that you do not know anything about that, that part about the order coming from the KLA to move? Now it's stated in the transcript but now you're saying something else. So am I right in concluding that you do not know anything about the order coming for the KLA to move or do you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Listen, it's not an order as an ultimatum. We received this as a message, as an information. The military structure worked pursuant to orders from their command. We were the logistics part. We worked on a voluntary basis and we received this as an information, as a message. They may have well given order to their zone commanders or brigade commanders or unit commanders. That I don't know. As I told you, the command, the zone command, was situated far from the hospital; and I'm not a person who ever liked weapons. So I didn't pay attention to that military part; I only paid attention to my job. I don't know to what extent you understand me. I just want to explain to you that nobody gave me any orders. My work was voluntary work. Had there been any orders, someone would have told me something when I left, and when they left with the wounded I joined my family, my wife and my children, not the KLA and their wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please answer my last question. You haven't answered it. Am I right that this portion of your statement in paragraph 11 is incorrect, that you do not have any knowledge about the KLA receiving any order, because it is stated here: "On the 2nd May the order came for the KLA to move," not that you move or your hospital move, but the KLA. Am I right in saying that you do not have any direct knowledge about that and that what is stated here, written here, is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I did say that, but as an order for the military part; as for us, logistics part, there was no need for someone to order us. We were voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I have been asking you all along. Thank you. Then your next question -- sentence in the same paragraph: "The civilians therefore also had to leave ..." Please tell me, Doctor, why did the civilians have to go if they did not take part in the fighting with the Serb forces? Why this -- the civilians therefore also had to go? If the KLA went, why did the civilians have to go?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Merely because everything that was Albanian was targeted and from what had happened earlier, the massacres that occurred earlier, we were scared and in a way we hoped that we would be able to arrive in Macedonia, Albania, or Montenegro and pass through Vushtrri. So the civilians left just because of fear, because the Serb forces, when they fought and when they burnt their houses, they didn't fight there in the battle-field where they can be killed, but they retaliated on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer whether the fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces were an everyday occurrence in this area?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Firing occurred very often. Now, whether there was just firing or exchange of fire, an expert can explain that. I don't know that. The hospital was very far from the front lines, be those in the north-western part or those in the south-eastern part, and, as I said, as a doctor I was only concerned with my professional work. On the critical night, the Serbian forces did not head towards the direction that the KLA and its soldiers took, that is, the Dumnice direction, but followed the convoy, the direction of the convoy. So those followed us from behind, whereas in front of us we were faced with forces from -- that were earlier positioned in Studime and Saracak. And that's when these massacre occurred, these 118 or 19 people were killed. We were caught like in between a pincer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: In the territory controlled by the KLA - and you mentioned many villages - which of those villages used to be inhabited by the Serbs? And I'm discussing the period before March 1999.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Maybe there were Serbs in Samadrexha because the population was mixed there. I think there were Serbs in Samadrexha until later. This is what I heard. I didn't see them for myself, but they didn't have any problems with the KLA until late. The Serb forces had their check-point in Llazoviq neighbourhood, and a little bit further up there were some households where elderly Serb people lived. This is what I heard. Before the war, I visited the area very often, Saracak area, but for the period you're talking about, in Saracak, there was no KLA presence. The Serb forces had their check-point there because there was a Serbian population in this village, in Saracak e Eperm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said Svracak, Samodreza, were there any other villages controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Saracak was held by the Serb forces. The rest of the villages were predominantly Albanian. They were not mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you whether in Gornji Svracak and Samodreza are there any Serb houses there, inhabited houses not just houses, but someone living in them.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I had several of them as my patients. I had good relations with them. I visited them very often before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serb houses there were in Gornji Svracak?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: About four or five, mainly elderly people lived there. The youth lived in Prishtina and would visit the elderly during the weekends. I mean, they had contact with the elderly people, their sons and nieces and nephews. I didn't see. But as I said, I visited the elderly people very often because they were quite ill. The youth would get employment in Prishtina or in Vushtrri or in other towns and would come in the village only during the weekends. So it was mainly the elderly people who lived in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how many Serb houses there were in Samodreza, please?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Up there in that neighbourhood near Malokve [as interpreted], the neighbourhood, I think there were two or three Serbian households, again elderly people; and the Llazoviq neighbourhood had more Serbian households, about 10 or 12, but I'm not quite certain about the number. The Llazoviq neighbourhood was closer to the town and a check-point was erected there on a hill nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm coming back to this paragraph 11 where you say that civilians had to leave after the KLA positions had fallen in Llap and Meljenica, which would be the Kosovska Mitrovica municipality, if I'm not mistaken, and you said therefore civilians also had to leave. Could you agree with me if I say that in such situations, given the rules of guerilla warfare that the KLA conducted against Serb forces, did civilians and KLA forces move together when they withdrew, and of course then the KLA members then would not be bearing arms?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's not at all true. The civilian population left in the direction of Ceceli and proceeded to Studime village. I was amongst these civilians, but I didn't have any uniform. I had the white coat when I worked in the hospital. There was no KLA member amongst the civilians in the convoy. As I said earlier, the KLA and their wounded went towards Dumnice, and I don't know where they positioned themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you were a member of the KLA and you were in that convoy and you were wearing a white coat. Do you know a person by the name of Bislim Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I didn't know Bislim Zyrapi. I didn't say I was in the convoy wearing the white coat. I said I wore the white coat when I worked in the hospital. I've mentioned in my previous testimony and statements that I was probably the only member of the KLA there. I had my doctor's equipment and bag with me at all times. I didn't see any other member of the KLA in the convoy, and I didn't hear from anybody to have seen a KLA member as part of the convoy. I don't know who Bislim Zyrapi is; my answer to your second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean you didn't know him personally or you never heard about Bislim Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I think I've come across this name in the newspapers or heard it on television, but I don't know the person behind this name. I never met him or saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now it's clearer. Could you tell me, when you read it in the newspapers or wherever, did you know then that he was chief of the Main Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There was no need for me to learn that. I was familiar with the people from the Shala Operational Zone. I knew them before the war, during the war, and after the war. I didn't know anyone from the General Staff. This was of no interest to me. I did not belong to the military part. My job involved human lives, saving them. This name I didn't hear in the operational zone of Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the KLA, did you know of an order that in the case of an offensive or attack by the Serb forces, all forces from the front line were supposed to withdraw together with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 3, paragraph 8, and on third paragraph on the fourth page in the Albanian, you say that: "30 to 40.000 people had fled to this area and that there was fighting between the KLA and Serb army almost every day." So based on that, am I right in saying that the civilians had fled to this area to avoid fighting because there was fighting every day, rather they did so pursuant to an order issued by the KLA. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm having a look at the English paragraph 8 and unfortunately I'm not able to find the reference to the paragraph Defence counsel is referring to. I wonder if he would be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said for the English version page 4, paragraph 3. I don't know what's written in the transcript because I'm not following it, my learned colleague -- I mean, the Albanian version. But just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe we may have the reference. It is paragraph 10 of the English statement; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is it necessary for me to repeat my earlier question?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: We didn't discuss this in detail. Order, yes, in terms of the military part. For us it was just a message, just an information, that we received from the soldiers that the positions had fallen to the Serb forces. We as civilians had to leave. I think there were about 30.000 or 40.000 people after the war according to the documentation found in the municipality of Vushtrri. This was the figure, 30.000 to 40.000 refugees. And I believe it is more or less an accurate number because that was a huge convoy, a lot of people. There was no order. Nobody could order me to do anything. We did what we did because of fear, because we panicked, we feared that what had happened to other people would happen to us. There was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph I believe in tenth paragraph in the English and the B/C/S versions, you stated, and I repeat it, that there were around 30 to 40.000 civilians. Doctor, I wanted to ask you: Did you ever gave a statement while you were in Montenegro in Ulcinj, to anybody in the latter part of June in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Where? In Ulcinj in Montenegro or in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In Ulcinj in Montenegro, 18th of June, 1999, did you give a statement; and if yes, to whom?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. It was a female representative of ICRC or International Crisis Group, I don't remember the name of the organisation. This was a woman that interviewed me, and another statement after the war in Studime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would be a convenient time. I'm sorry, I got a bit carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now then and resume at 1.00. Are you able to give an indication of your progress?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Today is my intention to finish my cross-examine definitely and to leave time for the Prosecution if they have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We'll resume then at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I would like D002-5212 to be put on our screens, that's the English version, and D002-5200, that's the B/C/S version. I would like us to go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is page 2, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. [Interpretation] We need to go to the next page in B/C/S. No, that page is not correct either. Next page, please. Well, obviously we have a problem with the document. It's the witness's statement from the 18th of June, 1999, and it's listed under this number. It's Witness: Shukri Gerxhaliu; Fahrie Gerxhaliu, the wife; and Florie Basholli. The statement was given to Muriel Rodriguez. You can see that on page 2 of this document, I have it here in front of me, but that's not what we're looking at on our screens. And it begins with witness statement incident 1-2, 1st of April. What I see here that's it, yes, but it's much further into the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you for a moment because obviously there has been a misunderstanding. While we're waiting for the proper document to be displayed on the screen, I would like to ask the witness a question so as not to waste time. We don't have much of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement that you gave to the ICJ -- to the ICG, the International Crisis Group to Ms. Muriel on the 6th of June, 1999, in Ulcinj; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was a lady I think of French nationality. I don't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After you made the statement, did you look at what you said on that day?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I didn't read that statement. I simply gave it and went home; but after that, she came back to me and verified the statement again with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that statement which we unfortunately don't have on our screens. I have a hard copy here in B/C/S so that I will have to wait for a while before I put to you the controversial part that I would like us to clear up. But let me tell you what this is all about, and I hope that we will soon have it on our screens. You speak about the incident number 1, it's the 2nd of April, and you say at the end of paragraph 1: "On the 2nd of May as we were going up and down from Sudimlja and back -- to Sudimlja and back again, in a field we were surrounded by members of the Serbian forces, the police and the paramilitaries, who came from Saljska Bajgora, Skocna, and Gojbulja." This is an incident that you spoke about a little while ago in your evidence when you said there were 30 to 40.000 refugees. You said around 20.000 civilians on tractors with all family members were getting down from the mountains, lest we should die?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: "Around 20.000 civilians on tractors with all our family members, we were getting down from the mountains lest we should all starve to death." Now, could you please explain the difference, the discrepancy in the number of refugees and the reason you provide for the movement of the column. You say here that you were afraid of starving to death, and a little while ago you provided another version. Could you please explain that, and in the meantime I'll look for the document.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: As far as the figure goes, I have always said that there were above 30 or 40.000. I didn't count them of course, but that was my impression of seeing them, and this is what I said to this lady. Maybe she made a mistake. Instead of writing 40.000, she wrote 20.000. Otherwise, I insist on this figure, about 30, 40.000. After the war, Simic was the deputy commander in Vushtrri and he gave the same figure, 30, 40.000 deputies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- refugees were gathered in that valley. So I don't think that there is any dilemma in the figure. It may simply be a mistake I think. In the -- in revising the statement, I made many corrections. This is one of them that I should have made but I have missed it. I didn't see it. This was something done by the ICG probably. That's why I'm here to say what I think, and I'm saying again that my impression is -- was and still is that the number was around 40.000. The mistake may be a technical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's much clearer. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best way to proceed according to my associate would be for me to show the witness the hard copy. If the usher could assist me and show the witness the hard copy that I have because I cannot now find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll wait a while. I wanted to tender this document into evidence, but I can't do it now. So I'll just wait a while. If I can do it, then I will do it; if not, well too bad. We've managed to clear up the controversial part through this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The second part of my question was in the protocol it says that you got down from the mountain lest you should starve to death and freeze to death. What was the actual reason? Let's clear this up so that it's clear. Why is it here in the ICG protocol?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There were several factors accounting for that, first, fear of eventual massacre, which, in fact, occurred. There were -- it was made -- there were no ices or snow and the medicaments, the food supplies were running out, but the main fear -- the main reason was prevailing fear of terror and massacre, which, in fact, happened later, as the case was in Drenice, in other places, where such -- Izbice, Racak, where such incidents occurred. Unfortunately this happened also in Studime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when you speak about the trailer where you were in that convoy, where you were hiding, can you explain to us what the trailer looked like -- in fact, let me be more specific. The place where you were on the tractor-trailer, how was it camouflaged? Can you explain that in greater detail. You've talked about it already but do it in more detail. Where were you on the tractor-trailer and what was around you or over you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The tractor had a trailer like all the tractors with trailers. There was some hay on the floor of the trailer. My family was there and the family of my spouse. Half the trailer was covered with a kind of nylon that could be extended, but, as it was, it covered half the trailer. And I was sitting in -- under the covered part. My daughter and the others were around me. So whoever came close to the trailer couldn't see me, for I was hiding -- I was hidden among the children and the family members. I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He's quoting in Serbian what the Serb forces asked them to do, that is, to hand over the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else apart from you under the -- this plastic sheet?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Only myself because that plastic sheet covered only part of the trailer on both sides and on top. It was myself and my daughter sitting next to me. The others were sitting outside this covered part. Myself and my elder daughter were sitting there. She was in front of me, I was behind her, and, as I said, it was covered by this plastic sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who drove the tractor?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The brother of my -- of my wife, Halil Bashota.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That would be your wife's brother "surak," that's the word we use in Serbian. Apart from your two --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, my brother-in-law, Halil.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to your two daughters, who else was in the trailer in plain sight?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There were my two sons, the mother of my spouse or my mother-in-law, Halil's children, Halil's sister-in-law, his daughters. The tractor was full with my family members and my in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see at all from underneath the plastic sheet?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: At first sight you couldn't see -- couldn't see me, but when they came closer with their flash-lights, I realised that they could see me. That's why I jumped down and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. Were you able to see anything as you sat there under that plastic sheet, anything outside of the trailer?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I could put my head a little bit out of that hidden place -- covered place and trying to see what was going on as much as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Things that were going on around the trailer, your brother-in-law being beaten up, the fact that money was asked from people, the discussion among the Serb soldiers about who killed how many people and who should be killed, did you hear all that, the conversation, from the immediate vicinity of the trailer, and did you hear the beating up as you sat there under the plastic sheet?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I could see and hear what was going on. And then on the next day I saw that Halil was beaten black and blue from the beating up as a result of the sticks being used. Mostly I heard, then I saw what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you jumped off the trailer you said that you jumped right onto the dead body of your neighbour or relative. Do you know how this man got killed or did you learn later? Did you know at that time what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, no. His tractor was next to mine, Haki's tractor, and I could see because his tractor was behind us. When someone said something in Serbo-Croatian and then he got off the tractor, and in the presence of his father, his spouse, his children, all this happened. Only a little distance separated my tractor from his, and he was executed there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, finally we can see on the screen parts of the statements taken by ICJ's -- ICG's investigators. I would like this page only to be tendered into evidence, both in the English version and the B/C/S version, that portion that I questioned the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe that the whole statement should be tendered if you want it as an exhibit because until its studied we can't be sure whether some other part of it might influence its content in the part that you've referred to. Do you want the whole document as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So be it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please tell me, what do you do today? What is your position, and what has your position been since you returned to the Vucitrn medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: After I returned to Vushtrri, I continued my job as a doctor of occupational diseases as a result of a training I underwent in Belgrade prior to the war. So I deal mainly with vocational diseases but also other diseases. After the war, I did a training on family medicine taught by some British professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Doctor, the last topic very briefly in my cross-examination would be as you said and we heard that you co-operated with the Lap Operational Zone; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I didn't have direct contacts, but there was a person we sent there for medical supplies. They gave us such supplies. They were better supplied than us. They sent these supplies through civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in is that whether you know that there was within the framework of the KLA both Territorial Defence and civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I simply worked in the hospital where I worked, treating patients. I said up front, and I'm saying now, that when it came to military aspects and organisation, I didn't even have the time to think about it. Most of the time I was working by myself, alone, without any colleagues. So I had to devote all my energies to health problems, epidemiological problems and so on, giving help to those who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you do not know about the extent -- existence of the Territorial Defence and the civil defence within the framework of the KLA; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I showed no interest in those structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And my last question: In paragraph 25 of your statement you said that some KLA soldiers helped to bury the dead. Could you please explain me why the KLA was doing so, why didn't the civilians doing that if it weren't for civilians who had lost their lives under certain circumstances? This would be my last question to you.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Are you referring to 3rd of May or 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On the 3rd of May, there were few civilians that had remained there. That's why it was necessary that the KLA soldiers helped them to remove the bodies from the side of the road. They told me to go back to the hospital because there near the hospital in a field about 90 cows had been killed, and I had to organise these soldiers and civilians to remove these cattle to avoid spreading of diseases. So there were, as I said, a few civilians there and that's why the KLA helped them to bury the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were those dead -- were they exclusively civilians or were there any KLA members, do you have direct knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: They were all civilians. I have the pictures here with me if you want to see them, and you can see for yourself that there was no soldier amongst the killed civilians. All were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you for coming here to clarify certain issues that the Defence thought had to be clarified, and hereby I conclude my cross-examination and I'd like to thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Gopalan, is there re-examination ?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, I have a few questions for you arising from the Defence cross-examination. You were asked why you left Vucitrn by Defence counsel. This is in page 35, line 24. First, to clarify, where is your home, in which village?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: My home is in Studime e Poshteme village or marked on the map as D. Studime. That's where my house is. Further up from my house is the Rashice neighbourhood where the Serb forces were positioned, whereas my house --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: -- is in the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And on the 2nd of May, why did you join the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: We simply joined the convoy hoping that we would survive. We had the paramilitary and military forces that had broken through the two front lines behind us and my wife always wanted all of us to move together so that anything that befell on us would befall on all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that night -- sorry, and on that day, in which direction did the convoy head?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: From Sllakovc in the direction of Ceceli, then from Ceceli turned right in the direction of Studime e Eperme, and from Studime e Eperme towards Studime e Poshteme, where it stopped near a hill. Behind that hill were the Serb forces that were firing every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. You were also asked some questions about where the various forces were located. You mentioned that on the critical night the KLA headed in the direction of Dumnice. Could you tell us in which direction is Dumnice? Is it north, south, or east, or west from where you were?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Dumnice was towards east. We, the convoy, moved towards Ceceli and turned right in the direction of Studime, whereas the KLA went to the left side, towards Dumnice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also mentioned that there were forces that were following the convoy. Which forces were these?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: These were the Serb forces that had broken through the front line in Shala, up there in Meljenica and in the Llap area. They had joined together the Yugoslav, Serbian, forces. At Sllakovc they were shelling, they were shooting, and we were trying to avoid them and we did up until Studime, where they caught up with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What were the forces that were located in Studime and Svracak?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Again, Serb forces, but they had been positioned in Saracak and in Studime from earlier at Rashice hill. So we had behind us forces that had broken the front line on these two places that I mentioned and in front of us the forces that had been positioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. I'll now like to move on to another topic. This is what you saw from the trailer or tractor that you were hidden behind -- sorry, that you were hidden within. Now, you mentioned seeing paramilitaries and certain soldiers extorting money, killing, and beating up people. Did any of these men appear to be searching for anything in the tractors?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: They would just come closer to the tractor, ask for money. Once they got the money, they would continue along the convoy. The next group would come. We thought, at the time, that once we give the money to the -- to one of the groups, we were no longer at risk; but we were delusioned because the next group would shortly -- after arrived they would search the men, they would beat them, and execute them in the presence of their family members just to cause fear and panic among the civilians. That's why more than 118 or 19 people were killed on that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. And I'd now like to take you to one of the men who was killed that night. You mentioned him in your testimony, that's at line 18, 9, where you say that you heard paramilitaries being asked not to kill their son and that this individual was executed. What I would like to clarify is the names of those whom you saw killed, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Haki was killed next to the trailer of my tractor. About 10 metres further was the trailer of Nexhip Bunjaku from Studime e Eperme who was killed. His father Sherif, he had married his son to a woman from another village and had joined the convoy on that day. And this is when I heard the Serbs saying to him in Serbian -- he first said to them in Serbian, Please don't kill my son. He just got married today.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: And then the Serb replied, We will celebrate the wedding now and executed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gerxhaliu. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You're most welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to direct your mind to the elderly couple. Now, who approached them? Were they paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: At the time of the execution, it was very difficult to tell; but there were policemen, paramilitaries, and other units that were well coordinated amongst themselves. But the police and the military carried out the most of the atrocities. The military joined them as well, so it was the police and the paramilitaries that carried out most of the atrocities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, you'll be pleased to learn that that concludes the questions. As I mentioned earlier, we have your full statements and your testimony from the previous trial as well as what you've been able to give to us today in response to the particular questions. And all of that will be considered by us at the appropriate stage of the trial. We would like to thank you for coming yet again to The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give. You may, of course, now return to your home and activities. The court officer will show you out, and thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was, I believe, clear and sincere in my testimony. The wish of my people down there, regardless of their ethnicity, is to render a fair decision. Thank you once again on my behalf and on behalf of my whole family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. We now adjourn and we resume at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
